name: Choose the next intervention
description: Choose the next intervention according to the strongest observed limitation; revisit this choice after evaluating it.
decision: what can I change to improve my solution?

children.name: Repair the pipeline
children.description: Choose the repair that matches the observed failure before comparing model quality.
children.decision: Which observed failure should I correct first?

children.name: Repair dependencies and device setup
children.description: Resolve imports, package versions, paths and device placement using a minimal failing run.

evidence.context: The execution environment has no internet access, so the library must be pre-uploaded as a dataset. The exact directory name and package version available may not match what the code expects, and different versions may have different module structures.
evidence.observed_action: Iterated through available bundled package versions by changing sys.path.append to point at different dataset directories (v127→v128→v129), then also changed the import statement from importing a specific function to importing the parent module (v129→v130: 'from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer, util' instead of 'from sentence_transformers.util import semantic_search'). Each iteration was a separate notebook run to check if the import succeeded.

evidence.context: A pretrained transformer model and its inputs must reside on the same device; if the model or input tensors remain on CPU while the other is on GPU, inference silently fails or errors out.
evidence.observed_action: Moved the model to CUDA with .to('cuda') and ensured all input tensors were also moved to CUDA before the forward pass, yielding a first valid LB score of 0.78177.

children.name: Match the model to its checkpoint
children.description: Reconstruct the exact saved architecture and tokenizer configuration and verify that all intended weights load.

evidence.context: An inference-only notebook loads pre-trained fine-tuned checkpoints and ensembles their predictions. Swapping the backbone size requires matching the hidden dimension in every downstream layer and ensuring the checkpoint weights were actually fine-tuned with the same architecture.
evidence.observed_action: Changed ROBERTA_PATH and TOKENIZER_PATH to a RoBERTa-large checkpoint, set HIDDEN_STATE=1024, updated all Linear layers in the attention head and regressor to match, and loaded new model weights. The large degradation (0.46→0.74) indicates the new checkpoints were likely not properly trained/fine-tuned for this task, or a mismatch existed between the loaded weights and the architecture.

evidence.context: Existing inference scripts work for prior model variants but a new checkpoint requires different tokenization, sequence bucketing, or embedding-layer adjustments that the old scripts don't handle.
evidence.observed_action: First tested exp307 checkpoints through an existing script (predict_exp302) with swapped paths (v99-v100), then wrote a dedicated predict_exp307.py script with proper tokenization, bucketing, multi-checkpoint averaging, and optimized rounding (v101), and finally tuned the rounding thresholds (v102). The dedicated script scored 0.82366.

children.caveat: Changing an architecture at inference is not a valid capacity comparison unless matching trained weights are loaded.

children.name: Verify checkpoint selection and file discovery
children.description: Resolve and verify every selected checkpoint path before running inference.

evidence.context: Model checkpoints are saved during training with one naming convention and loaded during inference with a potentially different one, especially after refactoring or running across multiple sessions.
evidence.observed_action: Added a print statement to display the resolved checkpoint path for each fold, identified the mismatch, and corrected the filename template to the actual pattern used during training.

evidence.context: When loading pretrained model weights from file paths, a small typo (e.g., underscore vs hyphen in directory names) can silently fail or load wrong/default weights, causing a large score drop without an obvious error message.
evidence.observed_action: Systematically checked and corrected checkpoint path strings (underscore vs hyphen typos) across all five folds. After fixing paths in v38→v39, the score jumped from ~0.30 to 0.383, confirming the path bug was the cause of the regression.

children.name: Join features and predictions by identifier
children.description: Restore entity alignment and the training feature schema before fitting or combining predictions.

evidence.context: A stacking meta-learner is trained on embeddings extracted from fine-tuned fold checkpoints, but test embeddings were generated separately (e.g., from a different run or exported once). A mismatch between train and test feature distributions can hurt the meta-learner.
evidence.observed_action: Replaced np.loadtxt CSV loading with calls to get_embeddings(test_df, checkpoint_path) for each of the five RoBERTa fold checkpoints. This scored 0.45924, slightly worse than 0.45816, but after further cleanup and adding RandomForest to the ensemble (v9), recovered to 0.45852.

evidence.context: Two models produce separate prediction files. One model is believed to be substantially stronger than the other based on prior validation or leaderboard scores.
evidence.observed_action: Built a merge pipeline: (1) write each model's predictions to separate named CSVs, (2) read both back, merge on essay_id, (3) compute a weighted combination of the two score columns with most weight on the stronger model, (4) round and cast to int, (5) write final submission. Iterated across v16–v20 fixing path bugs and adjusting blend weights.

children.name: Reuse fitted encoders and preprocessing
children.description: Apply each model’s fitted preprocessing and define handling for missing or unseen input values.

evidence.context: When integrating a new model that requires feature-specific preprocessing (e.g., computing discretization bins or normalization statistics), the preprocessing step must reference the correct data split variable. A variable name mismatch from copy-paste or refactoring can silently use wrong data or cause a runtime error.
evidence.observed_action: Fixed the variable name from train_fold_1 to train_1 in the rtdl_num_embeddings.compute_bins() call so bins are computed from the correct training split. This fix enabled a successful run and a large LB improvement to 0.69423.

evidence.context: A tabular dataset has many missing values and mixed types. A new neural network architecture is being integrated into an existing pipeline where simpler models handle missingness natively.
evidence.observed_action: Added NaN detection utilities that check inputs and outputs at each stage, replaced NaN values with safe defaults before channel construction, used careful weight initialization (e.g., Xavier/Kaiming), and inserted print/warning statements for numerical stability monitoring throughout the forward pass and training loop.

children.name: Correct prediction arithmetic and data flow
children.description: Verify numerical types, accumulators, denominators and the prediction object passed to each downstream stage.

evidence.context: An ensemble pipeline that collects predictions from multiple model groups per fold and averages them can silently produce wrong results if column names, group indices, or array accumulation are misaligned.
evidence.observed_action: In v8, fixed the column-group references so each averaged prediction column used the correct model-group prefix. In v9, fixed the iloc slicing and prediction list accumulation. Only after both bug-fix rounds did the submission score (0.79520) approach the earlier best (0.79600), confirming the bugs were the bottleneck.

evidence.context: A new model family is added to an inference notebook that still contains preprocessing and prediction logic for the old model. The two pipelines may transform features or combine outputs in incompatible ways.
evidence.observed_action: In v6, deleted ~248 lines of old preprocessing and Cox PH code, leaving only the LightGBM path. This immediately recovered performance to 0.67991 (new best), confirming the conflict was in leftover preprocessing rather than in the new model.

children.name: Correct metric and objective implementations
children.description: Repair callback signatures, direction, gradients and Hessians against the intended mathematical objective.

evidence.context: After many hyperparameter tuning iterations without submitting, validation scores may be unreliable if the metric function call has a bug (e.g., missing an argument), leading to wasted tuning effort on incorrect feedback.
evidence.observed_action: Enabled DEBUG mode first to run quickly, added storage for fold indices (ids_folds) and per-fold predictions (preds_tr_va), fixed the amex_metric call to pass preds_va as the second argument, then serialized fold artifacts to pickle files for offline inspection.

evidence.context: A custom metric (higher-is-better) is registered as an evaluation callback in a gradient-boosted tree trainer. The default early-stopping behavior assumes lower-is-better, which would stop training prematurely or at the wrong point.
evidence.observed_action: Changed the EarlyStopping callback to specify metric_name='QWK', maximize=True, and save_best=True, ensuring the best model by QWK is retained and training stops when QWK stops improving.

children.name: Verify the actual submitted predictions
children.description: Trace the real test rows through inference to a valid output file and reject placeholder or stale results.

evidence.context: A gradient-boosted tree model is trained and predictions are saved directly. The competition expects probability outputs but the model may output raw scores (log-odds) by default depending on the prediction method used.
evidence.observed_action: Applied sigmoid transformation to convert raw LightGBM scores to probabilities before writing the submission. Plotted histograms of both raw scores and sigmoid-transformed probabilities to verify the distribution looked reasonable. This fix improved LB from 0.76513 to 0.78358 (+0.01845).

evidence.context: In a multi-model ensemble pipeline, some models may fail to produce output files due to environment differences, missing dependencies, or memory limits. Without safeguards, the ensemble averages in missing or zero-filled columns, destroying the final score.
evidence.observed_action: Added a debug/check block with a list of known-good fallback submission filenames stored in a separate Kaggle dataset (../input/gq-debug/). For each model, a try/except attempts to read the inference output; on failure, it loads the corresponding fallback file, merges it into the submission DataFrame, fills NaNs, and normalizes. This raised the score from −0.004 to 0.304.

children.name: Isolate a failing stage on a small sample
children.description: Run a minimal end-to-end example with intermediate assertions to locate and fix the first broken operation.

evidence.context: When experimenting by commenting/uncommenting code blocks to switch between configurations, it is easy to leave imports disabled, pass wrong arguments, or use the wrong prediction method, each costing a full run cycle.
evidence.observed_action: Each fix was a single-line toggle (comment/uncomment) discovered only after a failed run. The author had to iterate through v16→v17 (predict_proba fix), v20→v21 (predict fix), v25→v26 (missing y), v26→v27 (missing import), v27→v28 and v29→v30 (fit call toggles).

evidence.context: A pipeline has several stages (tokenization, dataset preparation, model forward pass) and a change in one stage caused a large score drop. Intermediate outputs are not easily inspectable.
evidence.observed_action: The author made one small change per version: first updated the package path, then toggled the suspected cause (newline tokens off, then back on), then added the missing mask_token_indexes extraction, then added it to the dataset columns, then fixed its type from list to scalar. Each step was a single atomic change, converging on the fix in 5 micro-edits.

children.name: Check prediction parity after refactoring
children.description: Compare old and new pipeline outputs on identical examples and repair the first divergence.

evidence.context: A refactor that replaces live inference calls with precomputed predictions or changes many pipeline components at once can introduce silent errors (e.g., empty paths, wrong variable references) that cause large regressions.
evidence.observed_action: First fix the broken checkpoint paths (v119), then re-enable the full set of per-fold model predictions that had been commented out (v120), and finally swap the correct ensemble component (ensemble_2 instead of new_preds) in the blend formula (v121), recovering to a new best of 0.44803.

evidence.context: A pipeline is at or near its best validation/leaderboard score, and the practitioner wants to refactor scoring infrastructure or reorganize code without risking a regression.
evidence.observed_action: Bundled the numba acceleration with import cleanup and code reorganization into one commit. The slight score drop (-0.00015) was within noise, but combining functional and non-functional changes made it hard to isolate the cause. Subsequent versions continued without reverting.

children.name: Make comparisons trustworthy
children.description: Choose an experiment that resolves the current uncertainty about gains.
children.decision: What evidence is missing before I choose another model change?

children.name: Establish a measured baseline
children.description: Build a minimal valid end-to-end predictor and record its held-out metric before adding complexity.

evidence.context: Starting a competition with no prior submissions; the metric and data characteristics are known but no empirical signal exists yet.
evidence.observed_action: Built an initial pipeline (likely involving survival target transformation and GBDT/ensemble modeling) and submitted to establish a baseline LB score of 0.69332.

children.name: Resolve attribution
children.description: Choose between restoring a baseline, isolated ablation and a controlled interaction experiment.
children.decision: How should I disentangle the recent score change?

children.name: Change or ablate one factor
children.description: Hold the baseline fixed and measure a single component’s contribution with a controlled ablation.

evidence.context: Multiple changes (input preprocessing and model architecture) were applied in a single submission, and the resulting score drop could not be attributed to either one.
evidence.observed_action: The experiment was inconclusive about which factor caused the regression. In hindsight (v13) the author reverted both and re-added the head layers, suggesting the confounded change wasted two submission slots. Changing one variable at a time would have been more informative.

evidence.context: Each submission costs a limited resource (submission quota or compute time), and the search space of member subsets is combinatorial.
evidence.observed_action: The author tested removing a large batch of members in one step. The 0.00336 drop from the best score showed this was too aggressive. The subsequent versions (v14–v15) pivoted to a different approach (standalone inference), suggesting the pruning probe was informative but the author moved on rather than doing finer-grained ablation.

children.name: Restore the last verified configuration
children.description: Restore a known-good baseline after a regression and reintroduce candidate changes individually.

evidence.context: A post-processing step (e.g., converting predictions to ranks before averaging) has historically provided only marginal gains on the order of a small fraction of the total score range.
evidence.observed_action: Enabled CONVERT_TO_RANK in v12, recovering only +0.00067 (to 0.93790). This confirmed rank conversion cannot compensate for a fundamentally worse model configuration, and the author reverted the resolution/head changes in subsequent versions.

evidence.context: After modifying a scaling or rounding step in the prediction pipeline, the leaderboard score collapsed to the level of a trivially broken submission, indicating corrupted outputs rather than a modeling issue.
evidence.observed_action: In v15 the author reverted or re-applied the correct OHE and inference pipeline (handle_unknown='ignore' plus category remapping), recovering to 0.42097. The episode shows that an intermediate change that breaks the submission pipeline must be quickly identified and rolled back.

children.name: Test a small interaction grid
children.description: Evaluate a small crossed set of coupled settings while holding unrelated components fixed.

evidence.context: A single-parameter sweep has identified the best value for one regularization control (e.g., tree depth). The practitioner wants to know if combining it with another control (e.g., minimum leaf size) helps.
evidence.observed_action: After identifying the best single hyperparameter value via a sweep, re-sweep the same parameter while activating an additional regularization control. Compare local validation to the previous best; only submit if it improves. Here, the combination did not help, so the author moved on.

evidence.context: The practitioner has plateaued and is changing multiple levers simultaneously (aggregation strategy, checkpoint, architecture, preprocessing) across submissions, making it hard to attribute gains or losses to individual changes.
evidence.observed_action: Systematically toggled blend_strategy (rank→mean), swapped experiment directories, disabled NER/math preprocessing, and switched from BiEncoderEvaluator to CrossEncoderEvaluator. Each combination was submitted. All five attempts scored between 0.375–0.383, none improving on the prior best of 0.388.

children.name: Measure unchanged-run variation
children.description: Repeat an unchanged pipeline and compare candidate gains with its observed variation.

evidence.context: A tree-based or other stochastic model pipeline produces slightly different predictions each run due to random seeds, data shuffling, or floating-point non-determinism. Before attributing small score changes to code edits, the baseline variance must be known.
evidence.observed_action: Re-run the unchanged notebook 10 times and submit each result. Observe the range of LB scores to quantify submission variance. The observed spread was roughly ±0.0001 around the mean, indicating that score differences smaller than ~0.0002 are not reliably meaningful.

evidence.context: A stochastic ensembling step means identical code can produce different leaderboard scores across runs, making tiny improvements ambiguous.
evidence.observed_action: Re-submitted the identical code to get a second LB reading, confirming the score was at least as good (and actually better), suggesting the curation helped but the meta-learner's randomness also contributes meaningful variance.

children.name: Choose validation evidence
children.description: Choose a validation design based on dependence and distribution rather than leaderboard convenience.
children.decision: Which validation construction best matches the intended prediction setting?

children.name: Use target-stratified folds
children.description: Preserve class or binned-target proportions in disjoint validation folds.

evidence.context: The dataset has class imbalance and the competition metric differs from standard log-loss. Using random (non-stratified) folds and a generic loss for early stopping may not align training with the actual objective.
evidence.observed_action: Switched to stratified folds to preserve class balance, implemented the competition metric as a custom evaluation function passed to the model's fit, and shortened early-stopping patience slightly. The combination of stratified splits, competition-aligned eval, and moderate early stopping yielded the best score.

evidence.context: With few samples and a continuous target, random splits can create folds with skewed target distributions, causing noisy validation estimates and unstable meta-learner training.
evidence.observed_action: Binned the continuous target into discrete bins and used StratifiedKFold on those bins so each fold has a similar target distribution. Combined SVR and Ridge predictions per fold (averaged) to produce OOF and test predictions, printing per-fold RMSE for monitoring.

children.name: Use disjoint group-aware folds
children.description: Keep related entities or inferred topics together when validating transfer to unseen groups.

evidence.context: Group-based splitting ensures no group leakage but reduces fold count and may hurt when the test set mixes groups already seen in training. Stratified splitting preserves label balance per fold and allows more folds.
evidence.observed_action: Reverted from GroupKFold(7) back to StratifiedKFold(15, shuffle=True) with kaggle_prompt/difficulty indices appended to both train and test folds. This recovered performance to LB 0.82224. The author inferred that stratified folds with more splits and special-index augmentation outperformed group-based splitting for this data.

evidence.context: A stratified-group CV strategy is desired to prevent data leakage between similar samples, but no explicit group identifier exists. Text or other high-dimensional features are available.
evidence.observed_action: Fit KMeans on TF-IDF features (topic-based representation) to generate cluster labels as group IDs for StratifiedGroupKFold. Required multiple bug fixes: (1) exclude 'score' and 'essay_id' from clustering input, (2) use actual TF-IDF numeric data not column name strings, (3) ensure predict() uses the same TF-IDF columns as fit(). Set random_state=42 for reproducibility.

children.name: Audit subgroup-specific fold construction
children.description: Evaluate subgroup-specific fold allocation on a separate disjoint holdout, explicitly auditing any duplicated training and validation rows.

evidence.context: A known subset of training data comes from a different source whose label distribution differs from the test distribution. Simply weighting those samples during training did not yield improvement.
evidence.observed_action: First tried per-sample weighting in LightGBM (sample_weight argument) based on prompt/difficulty flags — did not submit (likely poor CV). Then switched to forcing flagged rows into both train and validation folds of every CV split, removing sample weights. This achieved a new best LB of 0.82080.

evidence.context: A special subset of training data (from a different distribution than the test set) was previously forced into every CV fold (both train and validation splits) to improve generalization. The logic was removed during cleanup, causing a score regression.
evidence.observed_action: Re-added the fold-injection logic that concatenates indices where kaggle_prompt==1 into both train_index and test_index inside the StratifiedKFold loop, and corrected the column filter from 'difficulty' to 'kaggle_prompt'. The LB result was 0.81752, worse than both v21 and v23, suggesting the fix alone was not sufficient or that other changes in v23 interacted negatively.

children.caveat: Several assigned experts duplicated subgroup rows into both training and validation; their reported scores do not establish unbiased validation quality, and that overlap is not recommended here.

children.name: Adjust held-out training allocation
children.description: Choose the holdout size during tuning and refit with more labeled data after selection.

evidence.context: The model contributes a small fraction of the final blended prediction, so its individual overfitting has limited impact on the ensemble. A validation split reduces training data without providing actionable early-stopping benefit at such low blend weight.
evidence.observed_action: Switched to fitting on the full labeled set (no holdout) for the final submission model, gaining +0.00008 on LB. This is consistent with the model being blended at low weight, so overfitting risk is mitigated by the dominant external predictions.

evidence.context: Feature engineering requires fast local feedback, but final submissions benefit from training on all available data. Maintaining two separate pipelines is error-prone.
evidence.observed_action: Used a simple toggle (commenting/uncommenting train_test_split lines) to switch between a fixed-seed holdout split for local validation during development and full-data training for submission. Verified feature changes locally first, then submitted with all data.

children.name: Audit validation against held-out rankings
children.description: Compare candidate rankings across local validation and genuinely held-out evidence before relying on either.

evidence.context: Multiple checkpoints are available from different training runs and epochs, each with a recorded validation metric. The practitioner wants to pick the single best checkpoint for submission.
evidence.observed_action: Systematically swapped checkpoint filenames one at a time across 11 submissions, testing different runs and epochs. None of the 11 alternatives beat the original v3 score of 0.96040. The best alternative was run 2516 epoch 13 (the original). Higher CV scores (e.g., run 0318 CV 0.9650) did not translate to higher LB scores (LB 0.95917).

evidence.context: Multiple checkpoints have been evaluated, and the mapping from local validation to leaderboard has been inconsistent, possibly due to distribution shift or different preprocessing between training and test.
evidence.observed_action: Swapped to a checkpoint with CV 0.9662 (the highest seen). The resulting LB 0.95870 improved over the immediately prior submission (0.95388) but did not beat the overall best (0.96040), confirming that higher CV does not reliably predict higher LB when the architecture or preprocessing differs.

children.name: Bracket a parameter using local validation
children.description: Use a coarse then narrower controlled sweep and reserve external evaluation for promising candidates.

evidence.context: A one-dimensional sweep of one hyperparameter has plateaued. Multiple regularization-related parameters (feature count, penalty strength, minimum leaf size) may interact.
evidence.observed_action: After an extended one-dimensional sweep of feature ratio showed no clear winner, the author switched to sweeping reg_lambda in one direction (20→50→100), found it unhelpful, then reversed course by jointly resetting reg_lambda to a moderate value and drastically lowering min_child_samples, effectively doing a coarse grid search one axis at a time and using the failure signal to inform the next axis.

evidence.context: A gradient-boosted tree model is part of an ensemble that recently achieved a new best score. Large hyperparameter changes (tree depth, regularization, patience) do not improve the metric.
evidence.observed_action: First tried a large hyperparameter jump (deeper trees, heavier regularization, longer patience). When that didn't help, incrementally relaxed one parameter. When still stuck, reverted most changes back to the previously best configuration and made only a small targeted adjustment (reducing the auxiliary classifier contribution), which yielded the improvement.

children.name: Stop a saturated search and change the intervention
children.description: Freeze the best reproducible setting when recent tuning gains are indistinguishable from noise.

evidence.context: A gradient-boosted tree model is already blended with a strong existing submission and the model's contribution weight is small (1–2%). The model is not the primary driver of the final score.
evidence.observed_action: Exhaustively tried goss→dart→rf→dart→goss→dart→rf→dart→rf→dart in rapid succession with occasional num_leaves/max_depth changes. After ~21 edits and 3 submissions, the best result was 0.79980, still below the pre-episode best. The exploration yielded no improvement and was abandoned.

evidence.context: Reweighting existing ensemble members yields diminishing returns; the blend composition has been extensively searched.
evidence.observed_action: Integrated prlnn-exp-01 as the primary/base model in the inference pipeline (loading checkpoints, feature preprocessing, forward pass), replacing the previous base. This yielded LB 0.69304, a +0.00069 improvement over v53.

children.name: Profile the prediction unit and data structure
children.description: Inspect entity histories, feature families and missingness before choosing a representation.

evidence.context: Starting a new tabular competition or project with a large dataset where each entity has a variable number of time-ordered rows and many anonymised columns.
evidence.observed_action: Loaded train.parquet, parsed S_2 as datetime, sorted by customer_ID and S_2, printed column groups by prefix, inspected NA counts and dtypes, then computed per-customer record-count frequencies for both train and test sets to understand the distribution (most customers have 13 rows).

children.name: Change the input signal
children.description: Choose between representation, selection and training-population changes.
children.decision: Which input intervention addresses the missing or noisy signal?

children.name: Represent the available information
children.description: Choose a representation whose signal is not adequately expressed by the current inputs.
children.decision: Which representation should I test for the available raw information?

children.name: Add entity-history summaries
children.description: Aggregate repeated records into recency, dispersion and range statistics at the prediction-entity level.

evidence.context: The dataset has multiple time-ordered rows per entity that must be collapsed to one row for a supervised model. Complex aggregations (multiple statistics per column) increase code complexity and risk pipeline bugs before a first submission exists.
evidence.observed_action: Started with a complex aggregation function, broke it out for interactive debugging, then simplified to only 'mean' for numeric columns and 'count' for categorical columns in a reusable function. This minimal aggregation produced a working first submission at LB 0.76283. Richer aggregations (median, min, max, last, nunique, std) were added back incrementally in later versions, jumping to 0.79348.

evidence.context: A large multi-row-per-entity dataset requires both understanding (EDA) and efficient preprocessing before modeling. Full data is slow to iterate on.
evidence.observed_action: Switched to a faster file format (Feather), sampled ~60% of customers for speed, performed EDA with plots on categorical distributions, imputed missing categoricals (add_categories + fillna), and built customer-level aggregated features via groupby. Then in the next step, removed verbose EDA cells and added sklearn OneHotEncoder and StandardScaler to formalize the pipeline.

children.name: Add temporal deviation or window features
children.description: Construct recent-window summaries or changes relative to earlier observations.

evidence.context: A baseline with standard numeric aggregations (mean, std, min, max, last) already performs well. A date column has been excluded from aggregation because it is not natively numeric.
evidence.observed_action: Tried several S_2 date encodings across ~10 iterations: per-customer max delta, global max delta with scaling, including/excluding S_2 from numeric aggregations, and finally settled on a simple 'last' aggregation of S_2. The intermediate submission (v10) with a buggy version scored 0.77194 (worse), but the final cleaned version (v18) recovered to 0.79274, roughly matching the baseline — indicating the S_2 feature engineering provided no clear gain.

evidence.context: Full-history per-entity aggregations (mean, std, min, max, last) are already computed from a variable-length sequence of records per entity. The model has plateaued and the task rewards predicting a future event that may depend more on recent behavior.
evidence.observed_action: Computed per-customer tail-3 mean of numeric features (groupby customer, take last 3 rows, compute mean), added these as new '_tail3m_' columns alongside existing aggregations. This yielded LB 0.79551 (+0.00059). Then swept: tried tail-6 window, tried adding categorical nunique over the tail window, tried replacing mean-diff features with tail3m-diff features (last minus tail3m_mean). Only the initial tail-3 numeric mean was submitted and confirmed as a new best.

children.name: Add targeted domain interactions
children.description: Construct a small set of semantically justified differences, ratios or metadata features.

evidence.context: Gradient-boosted trees can learn arbitrary splits and interactions internally. The baseline already includes per-customer aggregations (mean, std, min, max, first, last) and simple derived features.
evidence.observed_action: Over 12 versions the author swept many variants of 'after-pay' difference features: raw-level vs aggregated-level (_last, _mean), broad column sets vs narrow subsets (B_11/B_14/B_17/D_39/D_131/S_16/S_23), added and removed min/max aggregations, fixed suffix bugs, and tested mean-based interactions. None improved the score, so the features were ultimately commented out.

evidence.context: Gradient-boosted trees can learn interactions automatically, but the search space is large. Domain knowledge suggests specific multiplicative or composite interactions among clinical/demographic features that are clinically meaningful.
evidence.observed_action: Engineered HLA high-res mean, age/donor risk flags, comorbidity×Karnofsky interaction, conditioning dummies and interactions, graft×conditioning, a composite medical_risk_score, and age×HLA interaction. Also tuned Optuna ensemble search (weight lower bound from 0.0 to 1e-5, more trials). Gained +0.00178 to 0.68946.

children.name: Add text structure and linguistic statistics
children.description: Compute document or sentence statistics that express surface form, structure or linguistic quality.

evidence.context: A fine-tuned pretrained language model is the primary model, but the targets include aspects (e.g., thoroughness, formatting quality) that may correlate with simple surface features like text length or sentence count, which the model may not leverage well on its own.
evidence.observed_action: Built count-based features (word/sentence counts for question_title, question_body, answer) and host one-hot features, scaled them with StandardScaler, concatenated them with BERT outputs in the model, increased epochs, reduced batch size, and averaged fold predictions. This improved LB from 0.38324 to 0.38598.

evidence.context: The model already uses high-dimensional pretrained language model embeddings and sparse bag-of-words features, achieving a strong baseline. Handcrafted features (readability, syntax counts, sentiment) overlap heavily with what embeddings already capture.
evidence.observed_action: Added tokenization, stopword removal, POS tag counts, sentiment scores, readability indices, n-gram features, transition-word counts, and engineered ratio/interaction features. After observing a score drop, tried tuning loss constants and simplifying post-processing. The features were ultimately removed in the next episode, confirming they hurt rather than helped.

children.name: Tune sparse text representations
children.description: Add or tune word and character counts, weighting, frequency filters and low-dimensional decompositions.

evidence.context: A topic model with automatic topic count selection and remotely-loaded embedding models are used to create features for a gradient-boosted model. The pipeline runs but has not yet been submitted.
evidence.observed_action: Replaced remote SentenceTransformer model strings with local checkpoint paths for reproducibility and speed, changed BERTopic nr_topics from 'auto' to a fixed value (7), and adjusted clustering parameters (n_clusters from 6 to 5). This produced the first scoreable submission.

evidence.context: A text-based model uses sparse n-gram features alongside engineered features. The practitioner considers reducing the n-gram range to cut dimensionality and noise.
evidence.observed_action: Tightened n-gram ranges to reduce dimensionality. The score dropped, and in the next version (v17) the author widened them back, recovering performance. This indicates that restricting n-gram ranges too aggressively removes discriminative features.

children.name: Add frozen semantic embeddings
children.description: Compare adding or removing frozen pretrained embedding sources and retain only independently useful semantic features.

evidence.context: A stacking pipeline already uses embeddings from one backbone family and has plateaued. Another backbone architecture trained on different objectives may encode complementary information.
evidence.observed_action: Built a T5Encoder-based model with AttentionHead, extracted T5 embeddings for test data, normalized them, and fed them into the existing SVR/Ridge stacking pipeline alongside RoBERTa features. This improved LB from 0.45852 to 0.45773.

evidence.context: A gradient-boosted tree model is trained on concatenated embeddings from multiple pretrained models. Doubling the embedding dimensionality and adding more source models caused a score drop despite providing more information in principle.
evidence.observed_action: Reduced the number of LLM embedding columns from 5376 back to 2816 and removed extra transformer checkpoints. Paired this with shallower LightGBM trees (max_depth 5 instead of 8). The leaner feature set outperformed the richer one by a large margin (+0.008 QWK).

children.name: Add leakage-free auxiliary predictions
children.description: Generate out-of-fold auxiliary model predictions and join them as downstream features.

evidence.context: A practitioner has serialized models from earlier experiments and a current cross-validation training loop producing fold-level predictions.
evidence.observed_action: Loaded the pre-trained model pickles, generated fold-level predictions from each model set alongside the newly trained LightGBM, averaged the predictions per model group across folds, then blended all groups into a final prediction. This required multiple iterations to fix column-reference bugs and prediction accumulation logic before getting a valid submission (LB 0.79520).

evidence.context: A gradient-boosted model on hand-crafted and bag-of-words features has plateaued, and top solutions are known to use fine-tuned transformer regressors.
evidence.observed_action: Over five iterations, the author: (1) added a DeBERTa inference pipeline producing predictions as meta-features merged into the GBDT feature set, (2) expanded to multiple DeBERTa checkpoints averaged together, (3) switched back from XGBoost to a 15-fold LightGBM with tuned hyperparameters, (4) replaced glob-based checkpoint discovery with an explicit list of five fold-specific DeBERTa checkpoints each using its own tokenizer, and (5) cleaned up stray code. None of these versions were submitted, and the subsequent version replaced the expensive transformer inference with precomputed features and achieved 0.82433.

children.name: Encode metadata or paired text explicitly
children.description: Represent text fields or known metadata through separate streams, prompts or auxiliary inputs.

evidence.context: A fine-tuned transformer is already performing well on a text regression task. The idea is to give the model a comparative anchor by encoding each sample as a pair with a constant reference text.
evidence.observed_action: Encoded each test excerpt as a sentence-pair with a benchmark excerpt from training data, added a splitting mask to separate the two segments, and introduced an AttentivePooling module. LB worsened from 0.46533 to 0.46820. Then simplified by removing the benchmark pairing, splitting mask, and AttentivePooling, replacing with a simpler inline linear attention. LB improved to 0.46690, partially recovering but not beating the pre-episode best.

evidence.context: A fine-tuned text model uses only raw text but the dataset contains categorical metadata that may carry signal about the target distribution.
evidence.observed_action: Added a helper to one-hot encode the 'category' column, concatenated it with the BERT output, and fed the combined representation into the classification head. This improved LB from 0.38126 to 0.38697.

children.name: Test minimal versus domain-specific text cleaning
children.description: Ablate text normalization or entity-aware preprocessing using matched training and inference transformations.

evidence.context: A baseline model architecture already achieves a competitive score. The practitioner has a trained auxiliary model for detecting special text spans and wants to use it to improve input preprocessing at inference time.
evidence.observed_action: Introduced NER-based entity detection for text cropping in the cross-encoder pipeline, then toggled NER on/off across different experiment checkpoints over 5 submissions. The NER toggle showed inconsistent effects (sometimes helping, sometimes hurting), and the entire cross-encoder + NER exploration failed to beat the prior bi-encoder baseline.

evidence.context: When fine-tuning a pretrained language model on text that contains special whitespace characters (newlines, tabs), the tokenizer may split or ignore them unless explicitly configured, and inference must match training tokenization.
evidence.observed_action:
Imported AddedToken and explicitly added newline tokens ('
' and '

') to the tokenizer before inference, matching what the updated model checkpoints were trained with. Combined with the threshold fix, this contributed to the best LB score of 0.80442.

children.name: Test numeric preprocessing against native handling
children.description: Compare rounding, scaling or imputation with the learner’s native handling of raw values.

evidence.context: Gradient-boosted tree implementations can route missing values natively at each split. Mean-imputing aggregation-induced NaNs may destroy the informative signal that a group had too few observations to compute the statistic.
evidence.observed_action: Initially added fillna(column_mean) for numeric aggregates, then commented it out and left NaNs for the GBDT to handle natively. The final score (0.79274) was comparable to the pre-NaN-fill baseline (0.79348), suggesting native NaN handling was sufficient.

evidence.context: Tree-based models are invariant to monotone feature transformations and can handle missing values natively. Extra preprocessing adds pipeline complexity and can discard useful signal (outlier removal) or mask missingness patterns (imputation).
evidence.observed_action: Commented out the scaler, outlier removal, and group median imputation steps. LB jumped to 0.75825, confirming these steps were either unnecessary or harmful for the tree-based model. Later, adding outlier removal back in v38 did not improve the score (0.78971 < 0.79304).

children.name: Match and sweep image resolution
children.description: Test a small resolution range around the checkpoint’s training size with other inference settings fixed.

evidence.context: An initial baseline uses a moderate resolution and a standard fold count. Increasing resolution improves per-model quality; adding more folds reduces variance. Both changes are cheap to test at inference time when pretrained fold checkpoints already exist.
evidence.observed_action: Increased image size from 384 to 448 and changed fold count from 5 to 4 simultaneously, gaining +0.007. Then added the 5th fold back, gaining another +0.002. The best result used all 5 folds at the larger 448 resolution, showing both more folds and larger images helped.

evidence.context: A series of resolution probes has already identified a high-scoring resolution. The relationship between resolution and score is not necessarily monotonic, so nearby alternatives should be checked.
evidence.observed_action: Changed the test decoder target_size from IMSIZE[7] to IMSIZE[5] (a smaller resolution). LB dropped from 0.95705 to 0.94487, confirming the larger resolution was better.

children.name: Match image normalization to training
children.description: Apply and verify the checkpoint’s expected channel order, value scale and normalization.

evidence.context: Inference preprocessing (input resolution, channel normalization statistics) does not match what was used during training. This mismatch silently degrades predictions without raising errors.
evidence.observed_action: Increased inference resolution from 512 to 640 and replaced ImageNet normalization with dataset-specific values (mean=[0.4824,0.4824,0.4824], std=[0.22,0.22,0.22]). Together these changes yielded a +0.00639 improvement to 0.96509, a new best.

evidence.context: A pretrained model checkpoint was trained with unknown or standard normalization statistics. The current score has plateaued and the practitioner suspects a mismatch between inference and training preprocessing.
evidence.observed_action: Swept normalization mean and std values away from ImageNet defaults, submitting each variant. Every change hurt the score (best was 0.95760 vs. original 0.96062). The author eventually reverted to ImageNet normalization in v22 and recovered the score.

children.name: Adjust sequence truncation
children.description: Test sequence lengths that retain useful text within the checkpoint’s supported input format.

evidence.context: A single model checkpoint is underperforming a previously established ensemble baseline, and the practitioner is searching for easy gains without retraining.
evidence.observed_action: Changed SEED from 58→28 and MAX_LENGTH from 200→256 with the albert-xxlarge-r1-0454 checkpoint. Result was 0.4813, still worse than the best ensemble at 0.4652, confirming these inference-time tweaks did not close the gap.

children.name: Select or refresh features
children.description: Choose a selection intervention based on feature evidence and artifact validity.
children.decision: What kind of feature reduction or refresh is justified?

children.name: Tune the retained feature count
children.description: Sweep importance-based retention and keep a subset supported by held-out performance.

evidence.context: A tree-based model is trained on a large engineered feature set. A two-stage workflow is introduced: train once to measure feature importance, then retrain on only the top features. Validation scores (not public leaderboard) guide the choice.
evidence.observed_action: Implemented a two-stage pipeline: first train with all features to compute median importance across folds, then select top_ratio fraction of features and retrain. Swept top_ratio through 0.25 → 0.10 → 0.20 → 0.25 → 0.33 → 0.40 → 0.50, checking validation each time. Started aggressive (10%), found it too restrictive, then walked upward in small increments. Post-episode settled on 0.25 with added regularization.

evidence.context: A feature selection procedure already ranks and filters features, but an additional hard truncation limit was applied on top. The model uses tree-based learners that handle high-dimensional sparse features well.
evidence.observed_action: Commented out the line `feature_select = feature_select[0:4500]` to allow all selected features to be used. Score improved from 0.81614 to 0.81851, nearly recovering the previous best.

children.name: Ablate suspect feature groups
children.description: Remove or restore one coherent feature family and retain it only when it improves held-out predictions.

evidence.context: A gradient-boosted tree model is already performing well with a large engineered feature set, and the practitioner suspects some feature groups may add noise.
evidence.observed_action: Tested removing max/min columns (v68) and shift features (v69), which scored 0.78642—a large regression. Reverted the feature exclusions in v70, restoring all features, which yielded 0.79285 (new best). The experiment confirmed these features are valuable.

evidence.context: A working pipeline already computes a rich set of per-group aggregations (mean, std, min, max, last, count, nunique) that feed a gradient-boosted tree model.
evidence.observed_action: Replaced the cuDF/parquet pipeline with .npy array loading and simpler aggregations (mean, min, max, last two rows). Score dropped from 0.79361 to 0.79076, indicating the richer aggregation set was important.

children.name: Compare feature-ranking methods
children.description: Compare model importance and attribution-based rankings using identical downstream validation.

evidence.context: A more expensive attribution method (e.g., based on game-theoretic values) was already producing the best score. Switching to the cheaper built-in split-count importance caused a score drop.
evidence.observed_action: Swapped the feature-selection strategy from SHAP to LightGBM importance while also lowering learning rate and adjusting regularization. The score dropped further (0.79071→0.79056). The author later reverted to SHAP-based selection, confirming SHAP was superior here.

evidence.context: A previously better-performing feature-selection method was replaced by an alternative that led to worse leaderboard scores across multiple submissions.
evidence.observed_action: Reverted feature selection from LightGBM importance back to SHAP (top_n=202). This recovered most of the lost score (0.79127 vs 0.79056), confirming SHAP selection was superior for this pipeline.

children.name: Regenerate selection artifacts after input changes
children.description: Recompute or select the matching feature list whenever feature definitions change.

evidence.context: A feature selection step was previously run and its output cached. New features have since been added to the pipeline, so the cached list is stale.
evidence.observed_action: Switched from loading the precomputed feature selection pickle to re-running the feature_select_wrapper function, which evaluates all features (old and new) and saves a fresh selected-feature list. This ensured the new features could be evaluated and included if useful.

evidence.context: Feature selection was run offline and saved; newly engineered features are absent from the saved list, so the model ignores them even though they are present in the dataframe.
evidence.observed_action: Swap the feature-selection pickle path from 'selected_features.pkl' to 'selected_features_LLM.pkl', a variant precomputed to include the LLM embedding columns, so the downstream models train on the enriched feature set.

children.name: Change training examples
children.description: Choose data filtering, weighting or augmentation according to the observed population mismatch.
children.decision: Which training-population adjustment should I test?

children.name: Filter or down-weight noisy and mismatched examples
children.description: Test excluding or reducing influence of a justified noisy or distribution-mismatched subset.

evidence.context: An outlier list has been precomputed (e.g., via high-loss or distributional analysis) and the current pipeline is already well-tuned, so data cleaning is a plausible next lever.
evidence.observed_action: Loaded the external outlier ID list and filtered those rows out of the training subset before model training. This was a quick probe: two small code insertions, then a checkpoint re-run to verify.

evidence.context: A known train-test distribution mismatch exists because the training data was collected from multiple sources with different labeling characteristics, while the test set resembles only one source.
evidence.observed_action: Used the 'clean' variant (exp306b-large-clean) which presumably addressed the Persuade distribution mismatch. The resulting +0.00153 QWK gain on the leaderboard confirmed that aligning training data distribution with the test set improved this ensemble member's contribution.

children.name: Tune class or subgroup weights
children.description: Sweep loss weights or corpus sampling weights instead of assuming full inverse-frequency correction is best.

evidence.context: A classification task with moderate class imbalance and a non-standard evaluation metric that combines ranking quality with recall at a fixed false-positive threshold. A fast debug mode (fewer folds, fewer seeds) is available for local evaluation.
evidence.observed_action: Swept class_weight for class 1 through values 1→2→5→10→25→50→100, then reversed direction to 1.2→0.8→0.75→0.5→0.25→0.1→0.04→0.05→0.01, all in debug mode (fewer folds/seeds) without submitting. The sweep covered over 3 orders of magnitude in both directions from balanced. None of the 16 runs were submitted, suggesting the author relied on local validation to guide the search.

evidence.context: The raw class ratio can be very large for imbalanced problems, and using it directly as the positive-class weight often hurts. A fractional power of the ratio is a common compromise.
evidence.observed_action: Swept the exponent applied to the negative/positive class ratio for scale_pos_weight through values 1/2, 1/3, and 1/4. The cube root (1/3) performed best. Increasing the weight too much (1/2) or too little (1/4) both hurt. Kept the best-performing exponent.

children.name: Test synthetic feature-space augmentation
children.description: Evaluate interpolation or oversampling within training folds and remove it when validation deteriorates.

evidence.context: An ordinal regression model trained on imbalanced classes with a ranking-based evaluation metric (e.g., weighted kappa). The test distribution is known to differ from part of the training set.
evidence.observed_action: Applied SMOTE resampling to the training features along with SimpleImputer (mean) and a feature count cap of 4500. The LB score dropped from 0.81897 to 0.81098 (−0.008). The author later removed SMOTE entirely in v32→v33, confirming it was harmful.

evidence.context: A gradient-boosted tree model is trained on tabular features with an imbalanced subgroup distribution, and the test set is drawn primarily from the minority subgroup. The model has already been tuned on hyperparameters and feature selection.
evidence.observed_action: Implemented a mixup-style augmentation: for each label class, found nearest neighbors (first brute-force, then Annoy) among same-label samples and interpolated features to create synthetic rows. Generated 2000–3000 synthetic samples for underrepresented subsets and concatenated them into each CV training fold. Achieved LB 0.82295 and 0.82322, modest gains over 0.82250 but below the best 0.82432. The author later removed the augmentation entirely (v87), suggesting it did not reliably help.

children.name: Tune label-preserving image augmentation
children.description: Test geometric or color augmentation strength while preserving task-relevant image content.

evidence.context: A clean baseline pipeline is established. Medical images (e.g., radiographs) have natural variation in brightness/contrast due to acquisition differences, and the model has no augmentation yet.
evidence.observed_action: Added tf.image.adjust_brightness(img, 0.1) to the augment function. This single, minimal change improved the score from 0.94363 to 0.95160 (+0.00797), a large jump. However, hindsight shows the next version (removing/changing this) dropped back, suggesting the gain was partly from this augmentation.

evidence.context: A simple augmentation configuration already achieved the best score. The model architecture, loss function, and optimizer are held fixed. Only augmentation type, magnitude, and probability are being varied.
evidence.observed_action: Over 4 submitted versions, the author swept augmentation strength (brightness delta 0.1→0.9, contrast/saturation ranges narrowed then widened, rotation added then removed, application probabilities adjusted from 0.6/0.6/0.4 to 0.5/0.5/0.5). Each change was small and isolated. All scored worse than v3 (0.949, 0.944, 0.943, 0.944), showing diminishing or negative returns from augmentation tuning alone.

children.name: Change the learner or fitting rule
children.description: Choose the model, objective or training control implicated by the current diagnostics.
children.decision: Which modeling constraint should I change next?

children.name: Choose a model formulation
children.description: Choose a replacement or architectural change with a distinct source of predictive capacity.
children.decision: Which model formulation should I compare with the current one?

children.name: Compare pretrained backbones or capacities
children.description: Evaluate a compatible alternative pretrained backbone with its own preprocessing and weights.

evidence.context: The current best model uses a general-purpose pretrained backbone and has been extensively tuned on heads, image sizes, and post-processing with diminishing returns.
evidence.observed_action: Replaced the existing backbone with ResNet200D using chest X-ray pretrained weights, reduced image size from 640×640 to 512×512, used multi-head outputs, and disabled rank conversion. This yielded 0.96470, a +0.004 improvement over the previous best.

evidence.context: A smaller model variant already achieves a strong score. A larger variant has more capacity but may overfit or may not have been fine-tuned as well for the target domain.
evidence.observed_action: Swapped checkpoint paths from fit-v2→fit-v3 (v10→v11, LB 0.80432, slight drop) then from deberta-v3-small→deberta-v3-base (v11→v12, LB 0.80219, larger drop). Both alternatives scored worse than the original small fit-v2 checkpoint. The author later reverted to small and added fold averaging instead.

children.name: Compare boosting algorithms or libraries
children.description: Compare standard and dropout boosting or alternative tree libraries on the same features and folds.

evidence.context: A gradient-boosted tree model has been extensively tuned on tree depth, learning rate, regularization, subsampling, and loss function, with diminishing returns on the leaderboard metric.
evidence.observed_action: Switched LightGBM boosting type from 'gbdt' to 'dart' (a single parameter change), which yielded a new best LB of 0.79438 (+0.00121 improvement).

evidence.context: A gradient-boosted tree model with early stopping is already performing well. Dropout-based boosting (which randomly drops trees during training) is an alternative regularization strategy.
evidence.observed_action: Tried DART booster for several versions, then disabled it and reverted to gbtree. Since the best score came without DART, the author kept gbtree. DART's dropout-based regularization did not improve this pipeline, possibly because early stopping interacts poorly with DART.

children.name: Change pooling, attention or prediction heads
children.description: Train and compare a focused head or pooling change using architecture-matched checkpoints.

evidence.context: The backbone features are powerful but the classification head is minimal (global pool → linear). The metric is ranking-based (AUC), so better-calibrated or more expressive heads can help.
evidence.observed_action: Added an SSE (Squeeze-and-Excitation style) spatial-channel attention block before pooling (v7, +0.00266), then added a hidden Linear+ReLU+Dropout(0.5) layer between pooling and the final classifier (v9, +0.00135). Each architectural change was submitted first without rank conversion, then with rank conversion toggled on to measure its independent effect.

evidence.context: An ensemble of multiple model variants with different pooling/dropout heads achieves the current best score. The author considers whether consolidating into one model with a more sophisticated pooling mechanism can match or beat it.
evidence.observed_action: Replaced multiple model classes with a single model using learnable hidden-layer weights, mean+max pooling across layers, and attention pooling over tokens. v6 scored 0.48546 (much worse). Then in v7, fixed the layer weighting (softmax over zero-initialized weights, weighted sum instead of mean) and added a 2-output head with log-variance interpretation, recovering to 0.47432 — still worse than the ensemble at 0.47148.

children.name: Compare regression, classification and ordinal outputs
children.description: Compare output formulations that respect target ordering or independent target semantics.

evidence.context: The model's output layer uses a softmax activation (which enforces outputs summing to 1) paired with a multi-class loss, but the targets are independent continuous values, not mutually exclusive classes.
evidence.observed_action: Replaced softmax with sigmoid activation on the output Dense layer and switched the loss from categorical_crossentropy to binary_crossentropy, treating each of the 30 outputs as an independent prediction in [0,1].

evidence.context: A regression model with post-hoc rounding has plateaued on an ordinal target variable (e.g., essay scores on a fixed integer scale), and the metric rewards correct ordinal placement.
evidence.observed_action: Built a new inference script (predict_ordinal.py) that loads the same DeBERTa checkpoints but interprets outputs as ordinal cumulative sigmoid probabilities, sums them to get a continuous score, adds +1 to align with the 1-6 label scale, averages across checkpoints, applies optimized rounding, and tunes ensemble blend weights. This yielded LB 0.82736, a new best.

children.name: Probe direct language-model scoring
children.description: Evaluate a small direct language-model scoring baseline before integrating its outputs.

evidence.context: An existing pipeline with engineered features and gradient-boosted trees has a competitive score. The practitioner considers adding a large generative model's output as a new signal.
evidence.observed_action: Integrated a local Mistral checkpoint with PEFT/LoRA, ran inference on test essays to produce a 'mistral_score' column with parsing fallback, and prepared it for blending. The LB dropped sharply to 0.71784, a ~0.10 regression, indicating the LLM scores were harmful. The author abandoned this approach in the next version, switching to extracting embeddings instead.

children.name: Choose the fitting objective
children.description: Choose between label transformation, training loss and stopping criteria.
children.decision: Which target or objective change is supported by the metric?

children.name: Compare censoring-aware target transforms
children.description: Construct and validate censoring-aware risk targets, including subgroup-conditioned variants when justified.

evidence.context: A survival or ranking target is derived from a global statistical estimate (e.g., a cumulative hazard curve). The metric averages per-subgroup performance and penalizes variance across subgroups, so a globally computed target may under-fit minority subgroups whose event distributions differ.
evidence.observed_action: Created make_target_by_race() that splits the training data by race_group (0–5), applies the survival target transform (make_target) independently within each subgroup, then concatenates and re-sorts. Used this in place of the global make_target(). This yielded a small but consistent LB improvement (+0.00014).

evidence.context: Multiple monotonic transformations of the survival outcome (e.g., log time, KM probability) can serve as regression targets for tree models, and the ranking metric only cares about order, not scale.
evidence.observed_action: Tested each target variant in isolation by setting its blend weight to 1. Neither matched the prior ensemble, and the KM-probability target slightly outperformed the EFS-time target, but the difference was small and both were discarded.

children.name: Test consistent target centering
children.description: Compare fixed and fold-fitted target shifts with correct inverse transformations.

evidence.context: A gradient-boosted tree ensemble is trained with a custom objective on ordinal targets. A fixed global label shift has already been tuned and yields a strong score.
evidence.observed_action: In v104, replaced fixed global constants with per-fold mean/variance computation, subtracted fold mean from training targets, stored per-fold statistics, and recovered a global offset as mean of fold means. In v105, reverted to a fixed global shift (a=3, b=1) applied uniformly, removing per-fold centering. Neither version was submitted, suggesting the author evaluated locally and found per-fold centering unhelpful or equivalent.

children.name: Compare loss functions or objective parameters
children.description: Test a metric-motivated loss or custom-objective parameter while checking stable gradients.

evidence.context: A gradient-boosted tree model is trained with the default binary classification loss, but the leaderboard metric is a non-standard combination of ranking and threshold-based measures.
evidence.observed_action: Switched LightGBM objective to 'cross_entropy_lambda' and submitted. Score dropped from 0.79354 to 0.79317, so the change was harmful and should be reverted.

evidence.context: A custom objective function contains a tunable scalar that shapes the gradient. The current value was set during an earlier round and produced a new best score.
evidence.observed_action: Sweep the constant in small perturbations around the previous best value. The best result (0.82372) came from b=0.98268, close to the original 0.97268. Extreme values (0.001) and values farther from the original (0.94611, 0.96268) performed worse, confirming the optimum is near the original value with a slight upward shift.

children.name: Choose the early-stopping metric
children.description: Compare stopping on the true metric with a stable surrogate using the same validation predictions.

evidence.context: The default loss or built-in metrics of the training library do not match the competition's evaluation metric, so early stopping and model selection may be suboptimal.
evidence.observed_action: Implemented a custom feval function compatible with LightGBM's callback interface that computes the AMEX metric (normalized Gini + default-rate-captured-at-4%), passed it as eval_metric to model.fit with early stopping, and then re-swept feature selection to find the best ratio under the new metric.

evidence.context: The competition metric differs from standard losses available in the gradient-boosting library. The library supports a custom_metric callback that returns a name and a scalar, used for early stopping.
evidence.observed_action: Wrote separate helper functions for each metric component (amex_metric_top4, amex_metric_gini), then iteratively fixed naming typos and incorrect function references in the xgb.train call across four micro-edits (v21→v25), eventually settling on the top-4 component as the custom early-stopping metric.

children.name: Choose a training interface with required controls
children.description: Use the native or estimator interface that correctly exposes probabilities, callbacks and stopping.

evidence.context: A high-level API is already producing predictions blended at very small weight into a strong baseline submission. The practitioner wants finer control (early stopping, iteration selection).
evidence.observed_action: Replaced LightGBMClassifier with lgb.train using a Dataset, train_test_split for validation, early_stopping_rounds=50, num_boost_round=200, and predicted with gbm.best_iteration. The result (0.79973) was worse than the previous best, indicating the native API switch alone did not help.

evidence.context: Many gradient-boosting libraries offer both a low-level training API (returning a raw model object) and a scikit-learn-compatible wrapper. The two return objects with different prediction method signatures, even though both can output probabilities.
evidence.observed_action: When using the native `xgb.train` API (which returns a Booster), use `model.predict(DMatrix)` for probability outputs. Reserve `predict_proba` for the sklearn wrapper (`XGBClassifier`). The author fixed this by replacing all `predict_proba` calls with `predict` across OOF and test inference.

children.name: Adjust training dynamics
children.description: Choose a training adjustment based on convergence and generalization evidence.
children.decision: Which training control matches the observed learning behavior?

children.name: Tune tree depth and leaf capacity
children.description: Bracket tree complexity while controlling other settings and checking generalization.

evidence.context: A gradient-boosted tree model with default leaf count is already producing competitive predictions that are blended with a strong external submission. The dataset is moderately large but the model's own contribution to the blend is small.
evidence.observed_action: Added num_leaves=200 to the LGBMClassifier. The LB score dropped from 0.79980 to 0.79963, indicating the increased leaf count hurt generalization in this setup.

evidence.context: An ensemble of multiple gradient-boosted tree models is already producing competitive predictions, but a recent change caused a small regression or plateau, suggesting the individual models may not be well-tuned.
evidence.observed_action: Simultaneously adjusted multiple hyperparameters across all GBDT configs: lowered LightGBM learning rates, increased number of trees/iterations, tuned reg_lambda/reg_alpha, changed subsample ratios and tree growth policies, and added random seeds and device flags. This yielded a small improvement to 0.69332.

children.name: Tune penalties, subsampling or dropout
children.description: Adjust regularization strength against the observed train-validation gap.

evidence.context: After a feature-selection sweep plateaued without clear gains, overfitting is suspected and regularization is the next lever to try.
evidence.observed_action: Swept reg_lambda exponentially (20, 50, 100) while holding other settings fixed, observed validation results (not shown), found high values unhelpful, and reverted to reg_lambda=10 with min_child_samples reduced from 1000 to 20 to restore model flexibility.

evidence.context: After several rounds of incremental tuning, the practitioner has a current best configuration and wants to push further by adjusting two interacting hyperparameters.
evidence.observed_action: Tried dropout=0.25 with lr=3e-5 (LB 0.38012, new best). Then tried reverting dropout to 0.20 with lr=2.5e-5 (LB 0.37532, worse). Concluded that dropout=0.25 and lr=3e-5 was the better setting and reverted to lr=3e-5 in the next step. When a change improves, keep it; when it regresses, revert toward the previous best.

children.name: Tune learning rate with sufficient training budget
children.description: Bracket learning rate while scaling iteration allowance enough to compare converged fits.

evidence.context: A lower learning rate requires proportionally more boosting rounds to reach the same effective model capacity. If the maximum number of rounds is not increased enough, early stopping will halt training before the model matches its previous performance.
evidence.observed_action: Reducing the learning rate by 5× while only doubling the tree budget was insufficient; the model likely stopped before converging. The best configuration remained learning_rate=0.05 with 1000 trees.

evidence.context: Fine-tuning a pretrained transformer on a few thousand examples is sensitive to learning rate; too high causes instability, too low causes slow convergence or under-fitting.
evidence.observed_action: Tried 1e-5 → 3e-5 → 1e-5 for the learning rate while also adjusting dropout. The oscillation suggests the author observed instability or worse validation at 3e-5 and reverted, but later (post-episode) raised it again, indicating the search was not conclusive within this episode.

children.name: Tune epochs, rounds or stopping patience
children.description: Compare nearby training durations and retain the best held-out checkpoint.

evidence.context: After switching to a dropout-based boosting mode, the number of iterations must be tuned explicitly because the dropout mechanism makes early-stopping callbacks less reliable or inapplicable.
evidence.observed_action: Swept n_estimators through 2500→3000→3500→4000→4500, submitting at key points. LB improved monotonically from 0.79438 to 0.79537→0.79585→0.79596, with diminishing returns. At 4500 the author stopped increasing and reverted to 3500, settling near the best cost/benefit point.

evidence.context: The training set is small (a few thousand examples) and the model is a large pretrained transformer, making it prone to overfitting with even one extra epoch.
evidence.observed_action: Tested 3 vs 4 epochs; submitted the 3-epoch version which scored better, indicating slight overfitting at 4 epochs. Kept 3 epochs going forward.

children.name: Compare optimizer or learning-rate schedule
children.description: Test an alternative optimizer or schedule with otherwise matched training.

evidence.context: A smooth warmup-then-cosine schedule is already in use and the model's predictions are blended with tree-based models. The ensemble score has been incrementally improving but the neural network's training may not be converging to the best point.
evidence.observed_action: Replaced the cosine-with-warmup scheduler with a MultiStepLR that steps at specific epochs, added a flag to enable/disable the scheduler, and applied it at epoch granularity rather than step granularity. This yielded a small improvement to LB 0.69690.

evidence.context: The current optimizer and schedule produce a competitive score. A newer or trendier optimizer is available but untested on this task.
evidence.observed_action: Switched to Lion optimizer with MultiStepLR scheduling, but LB dropped to 0.69451. Then reverted to QHAdam, adjusted classification hyperparameters (reduced epochs from 5→4, increased LR from 0.01→0.05, set batch size to 256), achieving LB 0.69568, a new best.

children.name: Train and persist models with proper cross-validation
children.description: Replace ad hoc fitting with disjoint folds, best-checkpoint persistence and out-of-fold predictions.

evidence.context: Preprocessing code exists but no training loop or cross-validation infrastructure has been built yet.
evidence.observed_action: Built a 5-fold stratified CV XGBoost pipeline with GPU acceleration (tree_method='gpu_hist'), early stopping on validation loss, and fold-averaged OOF predictions. Included all preprocessing steps (imputation, one-hot encoding, StandardScaler) inline in the training loop.

evidence.context: An ensemble is already performing well, dominated by strong tree-based members. A neural network member exists but was trained without proper fold-aligned cross-validation or systematic hyperparameter choices.
evidence.observed_action: Rewrote the NN training function to use sklearn KFold, save per-fold model state_dicts to disk, tuned embedding_dim/projection_dim/hidden dimensions, and integrated fold-level predictions into the ensemble. Gained +0.00003 on LB (0.69350).

children.name: Average compatible model weights
children.description: Evaluate stochastic weight averaging across compatible trained snapshots.

evidence.context: An ensemble of fine-tuned deep models is already near its performance ceiling. Individual model weights from different training checkpoints still carry noise.
evidence.observed_action: Added `from torch.optim.swa_utils import AveragedModel` and made minor value tweaks, which together with the cleanup contributed to a new best LB of 0.45284.

children.name: Combine predictive signals
children.description: Choose ensemble membership, repetition or aggregation based on complementary errors and stability.
children.decision: Which combination change should I evaluate?

children.name: Choose ensemble membership
children.description: Choose expansion, replacement, pruning or restoration using ensemble-level evidence.
children.decision: Which membership change is justified by marginal contribution?

children.name: Add a complementary model family
children.description: Add one structurally distinct predictor and validate its marginal gain before keeping it.

evidence.context: Individual checkpoints show variable quality on a small, noisy test set, and the evaluation metric is a continuous error metric like RMSE.
evidence.observed_action: Blended three ALBERT checkpoints with weights [1/6, 3/6, 2/6] via weighted averaging, achieving 0.465 — the best score in the episode. Removing one model and reweighting to two models (4/6, 2/6) gave 0.466, still better than any single model. Reverting to single checkpoints always scored worse (0.488–0.517).

evidence.context: An ensemble of several gradient-boosted tree implementations (each with similar splitting algorithms) has stopped improving when new variants or blend-weight changes are tried.
evidence.observed_action: Integrated HistGradientBoostingRegressor models (trained on log_efs_time and log_km_survival_probability targets) with proper two-stage postprocessing, rank-transformed their outputs, and submitted. This jumped the score from 0.68643 to 0.69416, a +0.008 gain — the largest single improvement in the notebook's history.

children.name: Add diversity from training or input variants
children.description: Compare members trained on different features, targets or data recipes using matched inference.

evidence.context: A set of fold predictions produced with one data augmentation approach (pseudo-labeling) already scored worse than the best known ensemble. An alternative set of fold predictions from a different augmentation approach (input noise) is available.
evidence.observed_action: Replaced the pseudo-labeled RoBERTa fold predictions with noised RoBERTa fold predictions in the averaging ensemble. The score worsened to 0.49902, confirming that the noised variant was even weaker than the pseudo variant for this ensemble.

evidence.context: An ensemble of gradient-boosted trees and neural networks already exists. The same model family can be retrained with different target transformations (e.g., different survival-target encodings for a concordance-index metric), producing predictions that are correlated but not identical.
evidence.observed_action: Looped over a list of histgb target-transform variants, loaded each pipeline via joblib, generated OOF and test predictions, appended them as new ensemble member columns, and fed all into the AutoGluon ensembler. This yielded LB 0.69331 (+0.00119).

children.name: Select members by marginal ensemble contribution
children.description: Add or remove one candidate at fixed reference settings and keep the best supported subset.

evidence.context: A mean ensemble's score degraded after adding a checkpoint that individually scored poorly. No per-member contribution analysis is available, only the overall score after each submission.
evidence.observed_action: Removed the weak ALBERT checkpoint and replaced it with two albert-xxlarge-student checkpoints, expanding the ensemble from 3 to 4 members. This improved LB from 0.511 to 0.476, confirming that replacing a poor member with stronger, possibly more diverse members helps even in a simple mean ensemble.
