evidence.context: A meta-learner is stacking predictions from many base models. Some base models may be noisy, redundant, or poorly calibrated, potentially degrading the meta-learner's output.
evidence.observed_action: Defined a selected_features list to filter the prediction columns passed to the ensembler (ag_test = ag_test[selected_features]), removing weaker or redundant model outputs. This yielded a small LB improvement (+0.00003, then +0.00054 on re-run).

children.name: Restore validated ensemble members
children.description: Restore previously helpful members removed during simplification or debugging and verify the complete blend.

evidence.context: An ensemble of diverse model predictions had been achieving the best score, but aggressive pruning of members led to a significant regression, indicating the removed members were contributing useful diversity.
evidence.observed_action: Re-enabled all previously commented-out model/fold prediction calls to restore the full set of diverse predictions (v115→v116), then swapped one blend component from a simpler averaged prediction to the ridge-stacked ensemble_2 output while keeping the same 3/8, 2/8, 3/8 blend weights (v116→v117), achieving a new best of 0.44809.

evidence.context: Ablation experiments that removed ensemble members caused a score drop, confirming those members contributed positively. Simply restoring the old configuration would only recover the old score, not improve it.
evidence.observed_action: Restored the full inference/blending pipeline, re-enabled previously contributing models, and integrated a new pretrained neural network experiment (nn-exp-02) with proper imputation (KNNImputer) and scaling (StandardScaler) in the inference path. Added verbose logging to verify external model loading and predictions. This yielded 0.69070, a new best surpassing the pre-pruning score.

children.name: Compare matched checkpoint variants
children.description: Compare one compatible trained checkpoint variant at a time under fixed inference and record independently evaluated performance.

evidence.context: An ensemble of fold-averaged transformer predictions is already producing a competitive score, and new checkpoints (e.g., from multi-seed training) are available but untested.
evidence.observed_action: Swapped BASELINE_DIR to point to the roberta5seed checkpoints. LB worsened slightly to 0.45918, so in the next step, explicitly listed specific .pt fold checkpoint paths (removing glob-based discovery) to control exactly which folds were loaded, recovering to 0.45856.

evidence.context: Multiple checkpoints from different training runs or stopping criteria are already saved. Retraining is expensive, but swapping weight files at inference time is cheap.
evidence.observed_action: Performed a quick sweep: first tried ES weights (v11, not submitted but prepared), then default weights (v12, submitted, score dropped), then combined both (v13, submitted, new best). Each iteration only changed which weights were loaded, keeping all other code fixed.

children.name: Select fold or full-data checkpoints
children.description: Compare all folds, supported subsets and full-data checkpoints using independent validation.

evidence.context: When a meta-learner is trained per fold and some folds may have weaker base models or noisier meta-model fits, including all folds is not always optimal.
evidence.observed_action: Systematically toggled individual folds on/off by commenting out their predict calls and ridge model paths, submitted, and compared LB scores. Kept the subset of folds that scored best. With only ~7 public LB rows, small differences were noisy, so the author tried multiple combinations before settling.

evidence.context: A sweep over individual fold checkpoints has identified the best single fold. The evaluation metric is rank-based (e.g., Spearman correlation), so only the ordering of predictions matters, not their magnitude.
evidence.observed_action: Tried ensembles of 2 and 3 checkpoints from the same training run. Each combination scored below the best single fold (0.38871). Reverted to single checkpoint at v18 which matched the best score, then tried again at v22-v23 with a different combination, still falling short.

children.name: Reduce prediction variance
children.description: Choose fold, seed or input-view averaging according to the source of variation.
children.decision: Which repetition adds useful independent information?

children.name: Average more cross-validation folds
children.description: Compare fold count or flat versus nested fold construction, preserving disjoint evaluation and measuring marginal prediction gains.

evidence.context: Multiple changes (fold count, learning rate, number of iterations, model type) are being made together, making it hard to attribute score changes to any single factor.
evidence.observed_action: Reduced StratifiedKFold splits from 5 to 4, lowered learning rate (0.1→0.05), increased n_estimators (200→300), and rewrote the averaging logic to match 4 models. The combined changes (v5→v6) yielded only a marginal gain (0.78926→0.78979), suggesting fold count alone was not the bottleneck.

evidence.context: Predictions are formed by averaging across all CV fold models. The metric rewards ranking accuracy (e.g., Spearman correlation), so reducing prediction variance through more folds can improve ranks.
evidence.observed_action: Increased GroupKFold splits from 10 to 15 (while restoring lr=3e-5). This yielded LB 0.38610, a +0.006 improvement over the previous best, confirming that more folds (and thus more models in the ensemble average) helped.

children.name: Average independent training seeds
children.description: Train or load independent seeded runs and retain a repeat count supported by validation gains.

evidence.context: A single-seed cross-validation ensemble is already in place. Adding more seeds increases training time linearly but may reduce variance in predictions.
evidence.observed_action: Implemented a loop over seeds where each seed trains all CV folds; final prediction is the mean over all (seed × fold) models. Tested 3 seeds then 2 seeds; 2 seeds with the improved feature set scored best, suggesting diminishing or negative returns from extra seeds when compute is limited.

evidence.context: A fine-tuned transformer on a small dataset shows variance across seeds. A single-seed submission already scores well, and prior experiments showed multi-seed averaging helped.
evidence.observed_action: Used glob to iterate over multiple seed-specific model directories per fold, loaded each checkpoint, ran inference, and averaged predictions across seeds before averaging across folds. Also doubled the batch size. This gave a marginal improvement to 0.46533 (new best).

children.name: Average valid transformed input views
children.description: Compare deterministic geometric or multi-resolution test-time views while preserving labels.

evidence.context: A single trained model is used for inference on images where the target labels are approximately invariant (or predictably variant) under a geometric transformation such as horizontal flip.
evidence.observed_action: Added a second forward pass on horizontally flipped images, applied sigmoid to both outputs, averaged the two prediction arrays, and used the averaged result as the final prediction. The resulting LB score was 0.96342.

evidence.context: Deterministic TTA (e.g., horizontal flip with averaging) is already producing strong results on a medical image classification task.
evidence.observed_action: Added stochastic augmentations to the test transform pipeline and ran inference multiple times, averaging predictions. This dropped the score to 0.94671. The author then removed stochastic augmentations, reverted to weighted deterministic flip TTA (0.7/0.3), and finally commented out random flips from the transform pipeline entirely, recovering to 0.96835.

children.name: Evaluate stochastic dropout inference
children.description: Compare repeated dropout-enabled passes against deterministic evaluation mode.

evidence.context: Model weights are frozen/pretrained and loaded for inference. Dropout configuration is set in the model config before weight loading, but the model may be in eval mode where dropout is disabled.
evidence.observed_action: Tried hidden_dropout_prob = 0.25 then 0.50 in AutoConfig before loading weights. LB stayed at 0.46191 both times, showing no effect. The author later reverted dropout to 0.0 in v23, confirming the changes were ineffective.

evidence.context: A transformer model is loaded for inference. The framework's evaluation mode disables stochastic dropout layers automatically.
evidence.observed_action: Changed hidden_dropout_prob from 0.0 to 0.5. The score did not change, confirming that at inference time (with model.eval()), PyTorch disables dropout, so the config value is irrelevant.

children.name: Average compatible training snapshots
children.description: Compare predictions averaged across distinct useful snapshots with a single selected snapshot.

evidence.context: Each checkpoint variant alone may overfit or underfit differently; choosing one over the other can hurt the score.
evidence.observed_action: Tried each checkpoint variant individually (v11: ES only, v12: default/NOES only), observed the score drop, then in v13 loaded both variants per fold and averaged their predictions together, achieving a new best of 0.39071.

children.name: Choose aggregation
children.description: Choose fixed averaging, distribution normalization or learned stacking using held-out evidence.
children.decision: How should aligned member predictions be combined?

children.name: Use a uniform arithmetic average
children.description: Use equal averaging as a robust baseline when weighting or stacking gains do not generalize.

evidence.context: When ensemble members come from cross-validation folds of the same model, their quality is roughly equal, tempting a simple mean. When members differ in quality, weighted averaging may help.
evidence.observed_action: Changed aggregation from weighted np.average to unweighted np.mean when moving to fold checkpoints. The score did not improve, suggesting either the checkpoints or the aggregation method (or both) were suboptimal.

evidence.context: Two models are blended with unequal weights. A third, structurally different model is about to be added. The weaker existing model may become redundant once the new member joins.
evidence.observed_action: Changed weights from 0.6/0.4 to 0.5/0.5 as a preparatory step. This was not submitted alone; the real gain came from adding model3 in the next step. Hindsight (v7) showed dropping model2 entirely and weighting model1 and model3 equally (0.5/0.5) was even better.

children.name: Tune fixed blend weights
children.description: Optimize a modest set of fixed weights on held-out predictions and recheck after member changes.

evidence.context: One prediction source is known to be substantially stronger than the other, so the blend will be heavily skewed. Without local validation of the blend, the leaderboard must be used as the oracle.
evidence.observed_action: Sweep blend weights in small increments around a dominant-submission regime (95–100% on the strong submission). Submit several variants, observe that negative weights hurt (0.79957), that the optimum is near 1% auxiliary weight, and settle on (0.99, 0.01). The total gain is tiny (+0.00002 over baseline) confirming the auxiliary model adds marginal value.

evidence.context: An ensemble of several model variants has plateaued on the leaderboard. No new models or features are being added.
evidence.observed_action: Tried scaling up all blend weights (~×10), then selectively reducing some back to 1.0, keeping commented-out alternatives. Neither change moved the score, indicating the ensemble was insensitive to weight rescaling at this plateau. Abandoned pure weight tuning and moved to model hyperparameter changes.

children.name: Test signed blend weights
children.description: Allow a bounded negative contribution only when it improves independently evaluated residual correction.

evidence.context: During a blend-weight sweep, it is unclear whether the auxiliary source's residual information is positively or negatively correlated with the target after accounting for the primary source.
evidence.observed_action: Immediately reverted direction in the next step, returning to positive auxiliary weight. The negative-weight experiment confirmed the auxiliary model carries a small positive signal rather than noise or an inverse signal.

evidence.context: A brute-force or grid-search ensemble weight optimizer restricts weights to positive values. Some base models may be anti-correlated with residual errors of others, meaning a subtractive contribution could reduce overall error.
evidence.observed_action: Extended the weight search range from starting at a small positive value to starting at -0.5, keeping the same step size (precision) and upper bound of 0.51, so the grid search can assign negative weights to individual models in the blend.

children.name: Compare raw and rank-normalized averaging
children.description: Compare raw-score and rank-based member aggregation under the actual evaluation metric.

evidence.context: When ensembling multiple cross-validation folds of the same model architecture, the choice between averaging raw probabilities and averaging ranks can affect the final metric, but the direction of the effect may depend on other settings (number of folds, input resolution).
evidence.observed_action: Tested rank-conversion postprocessing repeatedly under different fold counts and image sizes. The effect was inconsistent and tiny; raw probability averaging was slightly better in most configurations. The author kept raw averaging as the default going forward.

evidence.context: When the evaluation metric is rank-based (e.g., concordance index), both the combination method and the post-processing of the final predictions matter. Ranking each model's output before averaging can distort relative magnitudes that carry useful signal across models.
evidence.observed_action: Blend ensemble members using their raw (unranked) predictions, then apply rank transformation once at the very end when writing the submission. Do not rank individual model outputs before averaging, and do not submit raw scores without a final rank transform.

children.name: Normalize member scales before blending
children.description: Compare raw, standardized or robust-scaled member predictions and retune weights consistently.

evidence.context: An ensemble combines outputs from heterogeneous models whose raw prediction scales may differ. Weight optimization is used to blend them.
evidence.observed_action: Added StandardScaler (fit on OOF predictions, transform test predictions) in v9, then submitted without it in v10 (LB 0.69400), then re-enabled it in v11 (LB 0.69408). Both scores were below the prior best of 0.69453, showing StandardScaler gave a marginal +0.00008 over unscaled but neither matched the previous best. The author later tried RobustScaler instead (v13, LB 0.69399), confirming that simple scaling of meta-features provided no clear benefit here.

evidence.context: When new model variants with different target transformations are added to an ensemble, their prediction distributions may contain outliers that distort a mean-and-variance-based scaler, degrading the blend.
evidence.observed_action: Replaced StandardScaler with RobustScaler for scaling OOF and test predictions before ensemble blending. This recovered score from 0.69376 to 0.69399 (v13), and further fine-tuning precision to 0.001 reached 0.69419 (v14).

children.name: Average within families before blending
children.description: Average related folds or variants into group predictions before combining model families.

evidence.context: A single AutoML pipeline already ensembles multiple algorithm families internally. Removing one family and training it separately introduces a manual blend step that may not outperform the AutoML's own internal stacking.
evidence.observed_action: Trained a second AutoML instance restricted to CatBoost only, computed OOF predictions from both models, grid-searched the blend weight on OOF using the custom AMEX metric, and applied the best weight to test predictions. Result was 0.79461, worse than the 0.79501 baseline. The approach was later abandoned in v9.

evidence.context: A well-tuned weighted blend of diverse prediction sources already exists and performs near the best observed score.
evidence.observed_action: The hierarchical blend (weighted sub-ensemble averaged with another sub-ensemble) did not improve over the previous best configuration. This suggests that adding an extra blending layer with roughly equal weights can dilute the contribution of the strongest signals rather than help.

children.name: Fit a regularized stacker on out-of-fold predictions
children.description: Compare a leakage-free low-capacity meta-learner against the best fixed average.

evidence.context: Out-of-fold predictions from both models are available, and a reliable validation metric can be computed on OOF predictions to select the blend weight.
evidence.observed_action: In v10, instead of using the external predictions as an input feature, the author kept them separate and ran a grid search over blend weights (0.00–1.00, step 0.01) maximizing the OOF AMEX metric between the AutoML predictions and the external XGBoost predictions. The optimal weight was applied to test predictions, jumping to LB 0.79588 (+0.0010).

evidence.context: The meta-feature matrix is low-dimensional (one column per base model) and the training set is small, so the meta-learner has very limited data to learn nonlinear interactions.
evidence.observed_action: Tried SVR (default params) first (LB 0.45969), then LinearRegression (LB 0.45912, better), then SVR with C=10/RBF kernel (LB 0.46423, worse). LinearRegression was the best meta-learner among those tested, suggesting that on this small, low-dimensional meta-feature set a simple unconstrained linear model outperforms a nonlinear kernel method.

children.name: Calibrate final outputs
children.description: Choose post-processing based on target support, bias and the evaluation metric.
children.decision: Which output transformation matches the observed prediction defect?

children.name: Map outputs to labels
children.description: Choose identity, rounding, optimized thresholds or distribution matching using disjoint validation.
children.decision: How should continuous predictions be mapped to the target support?

children.name: Retain raw continuous predictions
children.description: Keep raw outputs when clipping, noise or redundant monotone transforms add no validated benefit.

evidence.context: A rank-based metric (e.g., Spearman correlation) cares only about the ordering of predictions, not their scale. Without leaderboard feedback it is unclear whether clipping, rescaling, or leaving outputs raw matters.
evidence.observed_action: Iterated through multiple clipping/casting strategies (strict epsilon clip → [0,1] clip → no clip → float64 cast) without external feedback. Eventually settled on raw outputs with float64 dtype, deferring rescaling to a later version. The back-and-forth without submission suggests the author should have submitted early to get signal before iterating on post-processing.

evidence.context: A rank-based metric (e.g., Spearman correlation) is used, and a normalization step was inserted between model output averaging and a distribution-matching post-processor. The score dropped sharply.
evidence.observed_action: Removed the two normalization lines so raw averaged fold outputs go directly into the quantile-mapping post-processing. This was a prerequisite cleanup before switching model architectures.

children.name: Use simple fixed rounding or bins
children.description: Clip when required and use simple ordered thresholds as the baseline mapping to legal labels.

evidence.context: When targets take only a few discrete values (e.g., averages of ordinal ratings) and the metric is rank-based (e.g., Spearman correlation), mapping raw continuous predictions to the correct discrete levels can change ranks and improve the score.
evidence.observed_action: Iteratively adjusted per-column thresholds for mapping continuous predictions to discrete target levels (e.g., binary 0/1 flags, fractions like 8/9). Each version tweaked a handful of thresholds, submitted, and checked LB. Early rounds (v17→v19) improved score from 0.445 to 0.461. Later aggressive changes (v22→v23) caused a large drop (0.461→0.429), showing that incorrect thresholds can badly hurt. The author could not recover the peak score in subsequent fixes.

evidence.context: A rank-correlation metric is used. Some target columns have only two (or very few) distinct values in the training labels. The model's continuous outputs create spurious rank distinctions that may not match the ground truth ranking.
evidence.observed_action: Applied a threshold (>0 → 1, else 0) to the question_not_really_a_question column in the submission DataFrame. Combined with the domain revert, this contributed to recovering the score to 0.39004 (from 0.38280).

children.name: Optimize ordered thresholds on held-out predictions
children.description: Fit ordered cutpoints to OOF predictions and confirm them on data not used to optimize the cutpoints.

evidence.context: Targets take a small number of discrete values and the evaluation metric is rank-based, so mapping predictions to the correct discrete levels can substantially change the score.
evidence.observed_action: Applied extensive conditional transformations mapping continuous predictions to discrete levels for many columns. The rebuilt rules achieved 0.44173, a ~1.2 point gain over the broken baseline but still ~2 points below the best post-processed score, suggesting the specific threshold values matter greatly.

evidence.context: A regression model outputs continuous scores that must be discretized into ordinal labels, and the evaluation metric (e.g., quadratic weighted kappa) is sensitive to the distribution of predicted labels.
evidence.observed_action: Adjusted the threshold array to [1.61, 2.64, 3.49, 4.22, 4.78], compressing the upper thresholds. This yielded LB 0.82366, which was below the best but confirmed the pipeline worked. The author continued tuning in later versions.

children.name: Test target-frequency mapping
children.description: Compare quantile-based mapping to known target levels against per-sample thresholds.

evidence.context: Targets take a small set of discrete values, and the metric is rank-based (e.g., Spearman correlation). Continuous model outputs could be snapped to those discrete levels using the training-set frequency distribution.
evidence.observed_action: The author added per-column quantile mapping from train label distributions to discretize continuous predictions, but it produced no improvement (LB unchanged at -0.00372). The author then reverted to raw outputs. The lack of effect is likely because the underlying predictions were degenerate, not because the technique is inherently unhelpful—quantile mapping can only help when the base predictions already have meaningful ranking information.

evidence.context: The evaluation metric is rank-based (e.g., Spearman correlation). A postprocessing step that snaps predictions to discrete training-set values was previously beneficial with one model configuration but is being applied to a different set of model outputs.
evidence.observed_action: Disabled the quantile-mapping postprocessing block and submitted raw averaged predictions. The raw predictions scored slightly higher (0.37184 vs implied lower with postprocessing for this checkpoint set), suggesting postprocessing effectiveness depends on the quality/calibration of the underlying model outputs.

children.name: Compare global and group-specific calibration
children.description: Fit separate output mappings only for observable groups with sufficient independent calibration data.

evidence.context: Applying the transformation globally to all columns slightly degraded the metric compared to a curated subset. The overall metric is an average across columns, so per-column effects matter.
evidence.observed_action: Swept between scaling all targets vs. an explicit curated list. Scaling all targets hurt slightly (−0.001). Iteratively expanded the curated list by adding specific columns (e.g., question_type_instructions, question_not_really_a_question) one or a few at a time, checking LB each time. The best list scored 0.42449, confirming that selective column-by-column inclusion outperformed blanket application.

evidence.context: A regression model's continuous predictions are discretized via optimized thresholds. The data contains identifiable subgroups (e.g., prompts or topics) whose label distributions may differ, suggesting per-group thresholds could help.
evidence.observed_action: Built a separate topic classifier (sequence classification model) to predict essay prompts, then applied per-topic rounding thresholds to the regression predictions. LB dropped from 0.82319 to 0.81389, and a follow-up checkpoint/label fix gave 0.81373. The author later reverted to global rounding (v75-v76 reached 0.82461), confirming topic-specific rounding hurt.

children.name: Correct a validated prediction offset or orientation
children.description: Apply a justified sign, offset or reference correction and validate it on held-out outputs.

evidence.context: Ensemble predictions may have a small bias relative to the training target distribution. The test set is small and noisy, so aggressive bias correction risks overfitting to training statistics.
evidence.observed_action: Divided the mean_diff correction by the number of ensemble score components before adding it to predictions, effectively shrinking the calibration offset. This scored 0.45522, slightly worse than the best 0.45507, indicating the calibration did not help.

evidence.context: When a concordance or ranking metric yields a score near (1 − expected), the most likely cause is that the predicted scores have the wrong sign convention (e.g., predicting survival time when the metric expects a hazard/risk score, or vice versa).
evidence.observed_action: Negate the predicted risk scores (preds = -preds) before writing the submission CSV. The score jumped from ~0.29 to ~0.69, confirming the sign was inverted.

children.name: Calibrate output range before discretization
children.description: Evaluate a consistently fitted scale transformation when required by output support or threshold calibration.

evidence.context: Model outputs may be on an arbitrary scale (logits, unnormalized scores). The evaluation metric depends only on ranks within each target column, so monotonic transformations preserve ranking but the submission format requires values in [0,1].
evidence.observed_action: Applied per-column min-max normalization to the prediction array, mapping each column's minimum to 0 and maximum to 1, then assigned the result to the official target columns in the submission DataFrame. This yielded the first submitted score (LB -0.00372).

evidence.context: An optimized rounding/thresholding step already converts continuous regression outputs to ordinal labels. The thresholds were tuned on out-of-fold predictions, so the rounding already implicitly accounts for the prediction distribution.
evidence.observed_action: Added a MinMaxScaler fitted on OOF raw predictions, applied it to test predictions, then rescaled back to the 1–6 range (×5+1). Scores dropped from 0.82845 baseline to 0.82503 with scaling, and further to 0.80343 when replacing learned thresholds with uniform ones. The idea was abandoned.

children.name: Reshape component probabilities before combination
children.description: Test a temperature or power transform before blending and verify its effect on the combined metric.

evidence.context: When blending a neural network with gradient-boosted trees, the NN's sigmoid outputs may be too compressed near 0.5, reducing its discriminative power in the blend and limiting the ensemble's ranking ability.
evidence.observed_action: Applied sigmoid(2*x) instead of sigmoid(x) to the NN logits, effectively sharpening the output distribution. Combined with retuned blend weights and updated external GBDT scripts (inc13 variants), this yielded +0.00064 improvement to 0.69661.

evidence.context: Multiple models are ensembled via weighted averaging of sigmoid outputs for a metric based on ranking (AUC). Raw sigmoid outputs may be poorly calibrated or overly concentrated near extremes.
evidence.observed_action: Applied a square-root (power 0.5) transform to each model's sigmoid predictions before the weighted sum: 0.5*(pred200d**0.5) + 0.2*(pred152d**0.5) + 0.3*(predB5**0.5). This yielded +0.00037 improvement to LB 0.96679.

children.name: Apply a validated auxiliary or metadata correction
children.description: Add a confidence-gated or metadata-based correction only where independent evidence supports it.

evidence.context: A strong regression ensemble exists, and separately trained classification models that discretize the target into bins are also available. The idea is to use high-confidence discrete predictions to catch and fix outlier regression predictions.
evidence.observed_action: Built a postprocessing pipeline: load per-fold bin-classification models, compute softmaxed bin predictions, derive the predicted bin via argmax, compare with the regression ensemble's implied bin, and when the bin model's confidence exceeds a threshold, adjust the regression prediction toward the bin center. Started with a strict threshold (0.85), then loosened it to 0.58 to allow more corrections.

evidence.context: The ensemble post-processing applies a discrete bonus to the continuous risk score based on aggregated binary classifier predictions from multiple models. A new model has both regression and classification heads but only the regression head is currently used.
evidence.observed_action: Added 'prlnn-exp-01' to the condition that accumulates binary classification predictions into the ensemble post-processing, so its classifier output contributes to the binary boost rule. This recovered and exceeded the previous best, gaining +0.00010 to a new best of 0.69317.

children.name: Ablate and revalidate the current post-processing
children.description: Toggle the existing transformation on fixed predictions to measure whether it still helps.

evidence.context: A pipeline includes both multiple blended models and a non-trivial post-processing transform (e.g., rank normalization or multi-stage calibration). The practitioner wants to simplify the pipeline but is unsure which components are load-bearing.

evidence.context: The test data is stored in a columnar format and is several times larger than available RAM. The feature-engineering pipeline aggregates rows per entity, so entities can be processed independently.
evidence.observed_action: Split test-set processing into multiple chunks (initially 4, then 5 parts): use get_rows() to identify customer-ID boundaries, read only needed columns via pd.read_parquet(..., columns=usecols), process each chunk independently through the feature-engineering pipeline, run fold-model predictions, concatenate results, and call del/gc.collect between chunks.

evidence.context: Aggregated features from a large transaction-level dataset consume most available RAM, leaving little headroom for model training and test-time inference.
evidence.observed_action: Systematically downcast float64→float32, int64→int32, count columns→int8, dayofyear→int16; delete intermediate DataFrames (pk, X_train/X_test copies) immediately after use; insert gc.collect() after every major merge/delete; avoid creating temporary DataFrame copies in the CV loop by using index-based .loc slicing directly on the master DataFrame.

evidence.context: Extracting embeddings from several large models in sequence accumulates GPU and CPU memory from intermediate arrays and framework caches, risking out-of-memory failures.
evidence.observed_action: After each embedding extraction step, deleted large numpy/tensor arrays with `del`, called `gc.collect()`, `K.clear_session()`, and `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` to free both CPU and GPU memory before proceeding to the next model.
